records.text: 84. As of June 2025, the number of foreigners with work permits for the construction and marine shipyard and process sectors in Singapore was 460,300. These sectors are especially reliant on low-skilled foreign labour, as domestic uptake for jobs in this sector tends to be low. As Singapore prepares for more frequent and intense heat events, the country launched a heat stress advisory system in July 2023 to provide guidance to the public on prolonged outdoor activities. The Government has also reviewed sector-specific guidelines, for example for outdoor workers. The Special Rapporteur highly encourages this and complementary measures that prioritize the workers’ health and protect their rights. 85. Incorporating differentiated impacts and adopting an intersectional approach, as well as ensuring access to information and meaningful public participation, can greatly enhance the inclusion of diverse community needs and help guarantee collective well-being in the pursuit of a clean, green and blue city that harmonizes nature and people. During the visit, the Special Rapporteur observed that higher-income areas tended to benefit from better access to green spaces, more efficient public transport and cleaner air, while lower-income areas had comparatively fewer environmental amenities. Data were requested to confirm or deny this observation but none were available. A potential disparity underscores the importance of systematically documenting socioeconomic differences and integrating such data into urban planning and environmental policymaking. By doing so, Singapore can ensure that environmental benefits and protections are equitably distributed and that preventive measures are in place to avoid discrimination and environmental injustice.

records.text: 83. Singapore faces one of the lowest fertility rates globally (1.15 children per woman), alongside rising life expectancy, leading to a rapidly ageing population and a shrinking youth demographic. By 2030, about 1 in 4 Singaporeans will be aged 65 or above, up from 1 in 10 in 2010. To prepare for this major demographic challenge, the Ministerial Committee on Ageing was established in 2007, bringing together multiple government agencies to coordinate efforts relating to population ageing. Older persons in Singapore face heightened vulnerability to climate impacts due to a combination of physiological changes, pre-existing health conditions and socioeconomic factors. Older individuals may have a diminished perception of discomfort in hot environments, leading them to underestimate the risks associated with high temperatures. Climate change also exacerbates existing health conditions that are prevalent among older adults: extreme heat can worsen common age‐related ailments such as heart, lung and kidney disease. Air pollution also has more serious effects on older people and increases health risks, including in relation to dementia. Singapore must therefore consider these intersecting factors in a more comprehensive manner to strengthen prevention and protection measures, including those addressing the underlying drivers of contamination.

records.text: 82. Environmental and climate impacts affect everyone, although they have a disproportionately greater impact on those in situations of vulnerability. Many current government policies and programmes include people in vulnerable situations, such as older persons, in particular those with dementia, children, in particular with regard to air pollution, and outdoor workers, with regard to heat. Singapore should further consider differentiated impacts from environmental and climate change, including from heat, air pollution and sea‐level rise, in its planning and measures. Special emphasis should be placed on gender‐based impacts that are yet to be considered and can strengthen and increase the efficiency of current efforts, as well as including people with disabilities, people who work outdoors, migrant workers (working outdoors in construction or in shipyards) and people from low-income communities.

records.text: Obligation to effectively monitor businesses and for businesses to respect human rights, including the environment 80. States have an obligation to regulate and effectively monitor business activities operating under their jurisdiction, including those domiciled within their territory but conducting operations abroad. This responsibility stems from well-established principles of international law and human rights frameworks, which emphasize that States must ensure that corporate conduct under their jurisdiction does not contribute to environmental degradation or human rights violations, regardless of where such impacts occur. In this regard, several international bodies have reiterated that States, including Singapore, should strengthen their oversight mechanisms to ensure that enterprises headquartered or registered in their territory are held accountable for their actions overseas. This includes adopting clear regulatory frameworks, due diligence requirements and monitoring systems to prevent and address adverse environmental and climate-related impacts throughout global value chains. Given the position of Singapore as an international business hub, it is important that the country pays close attention to this issue to prevent adverse effects on the right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment. 81. The International Court of Justice has warned that obligations to protect the climate system and the environment from greenhouse gas emissions are binding for all States and require effective regulation of private actors and meaningful international cooperation. Several special procedures have urged Singapore to integrate human rights considerations for businesses registered there. The Special Rapporteur highlights the potential impacts on the right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment and the need to pay attention to it, in particular given the position and importance of Singapore as an international business hub.

records.section: Procedural elements of the right to a healthy environment
records.text: 75. Access to information, public participation and access to justice are recognized human rights and essential elements of the right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment. Information is also fundamental to understanding how environmental harms have differentiated impacts on individuals and groups of people, depending on their situation of vulnerability. States should proactively provide for and facilitate public participation, consider the views of the public in decision-making process and grant access to justice to solve conflicts. This contributes to more effective decisions and more involvement from the population and thus strengthens the rule of law and accountability. 76. The Planning Act and Planning (Master Plan) Rules allow for public review of changes, feedback and hearings. Information and participation are included in the Draft Master Plan and the Long-Term Plan. While there is no express regulation regarding access to information and public participation, the Special Rapporteur was informed by representatives of the Government, members of civil society and people from different communities that spaces for engagement had increased in the previous decade, which was viewed as positive. The main reason identified for that improvement was the willingness and leadership of some government officials, given the lack of dedicated legislation and regulations. 77. Regulation of and further clarification on processes, criteria and opportunities for accessing information and public participation are crucial and significantly benefit national sustainability efforts and human rights. Noting that Singapore has facilitated public dialogues to contribute to its environmental and climate initiatives, such as in the case of public consultations launched by the National Climate Change Secretariat, the Government should further ensure that public information is available and accessible and that public participation is timely and effective. For example, information, such as that contained in environmental impact assessments, should be fully available. 78. The Special Rapporteur was informed that people, including youth, had reportedly been excluded from participating in certain processes because their opinions were perceived as divergent from dominant narratives. Information was received on cases of youth being subject to police investigation following appearances on social media holding signs on climate action. It is important for the Government to strengthen and continue efforts to increase public participation and protect the freedom of expression, especially of youth. Singapore should accept feedback and explain its decisions while keeping spaces open for dialogue. Information and public participation are rights and key for “green citizenry”, as the Government describes it, including in relation to youth and children, in local, national and international forums. 79. Lastly, considering the important role of businesses and environmental and climate impacts, special attention should be paid to the role of businesses, which should be scrutinized and potential greenwashing detected and prevented. Science has shown that not all environmental and climate impacts can be offset or economically valued and that some are irreversible. This underscores the limitations of relying solely on market-based or compensatory mechanisms to address environmental harm. Efforts for corporate responsibility and accountability should be further advanced, including by increased transparency, information-sharing on business activities and their impacts on value chains, including in relation with climate reporting, and climate actions such as climate finance.

records.text: 71. Access to safe and sufficient water is vital for the right to a healthy environment. Singapore has achieved an impressive 100 per cent coverage of the population of drinking water and sanitation. Water sources include 250 million gallons per day of water imported from Malaysia under the 1962 Water Agreement, which will expire in 2061, local water catchment, desalinization plants and recycled water treatment. Since 2011, the water catchment area of Singapore increased from half to two thirds of the country’s land surface, becoming one of the few countries in the world to harvest urban stormwater on a large scale for potable consumption. 72. Water management in Singapore encompasses a concurrent emphasis on supply and demand management, including wastewater and stormwater management, institutional effectiveness and effective legal and regulatory frameworks. The entire water cycle is managed by the Public Utilities Board, which is also in charge of coastal protection. In terms of the affordability of drinking water, Singapore offers schemes to help offset rising utility bills, including rebates and climate vouchers for energy and water efficiency. 73. According to information provided to the Special Rapporteur by the Public Utilities Board during the visit, non-domestic water demand (including industrial) is projected to increase from half of the total water consumption in Singapore to about two thirds by 2065. Water pricing has been central to water demand management, with a two-tier tariff that applies a higher rate to larger water users, which are typically from the non-domestic sector. As pricing of water will not guarantee a decrease in water use by industry, and in the context of climate change, water scarcity and toxic pollution, additional measures to reduce water demand and increase efficiency in industrial use should be further strengthened to ensure the sustainable use of water sources. A sustainable future requires curbing and managing energy and water demand in all sectors, including for artificial intelligence and the rise of cryptocurrencies. Human rights- and ecosystem-based approaches should be included, recognizing that water is a natural resource and that access to it a human right. 74. These complementary approaches are particularly important considering the existence of and potential increase in operational data centres, which use large amounts of water and energy. Consequently, it is essential for Singapore to consider best available science and planetary boundaries related to water consumption and ensure that adequate regulation and monitoring of businesses are in place, including through schemes to reduce demand, avoiding continued and increased use of fossil fuel energy that aggravates climate change and worsens current and future social, environmental and human rights impacts.

records.text: Non-toxic environments where people can live, work, learn and play 66. A healthy environment includes the right for everyone to enjoy non-toxic environments and is directly related to waste production and its management, among other aspects. 67. The National Environment Agency plans, develops and administers the solid and hazardous waste management systems of Singapore, including licensing and regulatory functions to ensure that waste is properly collected, treated and disposed of. The integrated solid waste management system of Singapore is focused on reducing, reusing and recycling. Waste-to-energy incineration plants have been selected as the best technical solution as they reduce waste volume efficiently to conserve landfill space. Singapore uses some of the world’s most advanced waste management systems. 68. Currently, about 90 per cent of solid waste is incinerated, generating about 2 per cent of the country’s electricity. Approximately 2,000 tons of solid waste per day, including incineration ash and non-incinerable waste, are disposed of on Semakau Island, where the only active landfill is located. The Government estimates that this landfill will be full by 2035: reducing waste is therefore essential. Singapore aims to reduce the amount of waste sent to landfill by 20 per cent per person by 2026, and 30 per cent by 2030. To achieve this, efforts to reduce waste, including food and plastic waste, and improved separation of waste should be prioritized, focusing on the sectors and businesses producing most waste. It is also necessary to assess and address the environmental impacts of Semakau Island, which was created through land reclamation, and further advance restoration measures there. These actions are consistent with the State’s obligations under international environmental law, including the duty to prevent environmental harm and to ensure restoration where degradation has occurred, including in the ocean and marine environments. 69. Plastic use and, thus, plastic waste are considerable issues in Singapore. In 2023, only 5 per cent of 957,000 tons of plastic waste was recycled; the remainder was incinerated. Packaging waste accounts for about one third of all domestic waste and over 50 per cent of packaging is plastic. Singapore aims to increase its recycling rate to 70 per cent by 2030. Other measures have been implemented, including a mandatory packaging reporting regime, launched in 2021, requiring producers of packaged products and retailers with an annual turnover of more than US$7.7 million to disclose packaging data and waste management plans. A programme on extended producer responsibility for beverage containers will start on 1 April 2026. In addition, a 5-cent disposable carrier bag charge at major supermarkets, implemented in July 2023, has encouraged over 90 per cent of shoppers to bring their own bags. 70. The Special Rapporteur strongly recommends that the Government and businesses implement a whole-of-cycle perspective, urgently find ways to stop using single-use plastic and advance other measures to significantly reduce plastic production and consumption, and that individuals also support such measures. Reducing plastic waste will increase waste management efficiency while helping to achieve zero-waste targets. It will also benefit the health of the population and nature of Singapore, tackling climate change and improving marine conservation, air quality and a safe climate.

records.text: 61. Healthy and sustainably produced food, as part of the human right to a healthy environment, implies that food production does not cause environmental or human health harms and guarantees the protection of food systems. 62. Considering its constraints in terms of land, Singapore relies heavily on importing food: more than 90 per cent of its food is imported. Some food travels long distances, which increases carbon emissions and potential environmental impacts. It also renders Singapore susceptible to supply disruptions linked to factors such as extreme global weather events and geopolitical tensions and could be worsened by increasing climate impacts. 63. In 2019, the goal of producing 30 per cent of food locally was set in the Food Agenda of Singapore, aligned with the 2019 Master Plan. Unfortunately, in 2024, local production of vegetables and seafood fell, setting back its goal. The decline followed disruptions in the farming sector, including closures of major players and delays or downsizing of production plans. As a result, local food output accounted for less than 10 per cent of demand, with both vegetable farming and aquaculture showing declines since 2021. 64. According to information received during the visit, food governmental production strategies seem to rely on high-technology research and aquaculture-related activities. Increasing consideration of natural sources, traditional ways of production, ancestral knowledge, permaculture and other kinds of sustainable food production systems is important for improving overall sustainability and reducing water and energy demands, while reducing climate impacts and promoting healthy biodiversity and ecosystems. For example, the Special Rapporteur met with persons who had taken the initiative to grow their own food. They mentioned a lack of government support for their initiatives, despite the opportunity of local food gardens to contribute to an increase in local food production. Given existing challenges, initiatives like this should be supported to help achieve goals of local food production, while benefiting from natural solutions and ancestral knowledge. 65. Considering the need to import food, it is important to recall the responsibility of the State to ensure that imported food is produced in an environmentally sustainable manner. This entails strengthening certification systems and implementing adequate monitoring mechanisms to prevent imported food from exacerbating climate change, such as through the indirect promotion of deforestation and other unsustainable land-use practices. Food imports should contribute to the protection of human rights and the environment where the food is produced. Given the high levels of food waste in Singapore (784,000 tonnes in 2024), prioritizing strategies to reduce waste is essential for enhancing food system sustainability and mitigating associated environmental impacts.

records.text: 50. Healthy ecosystems and biodiversity are vital for all beings and essential to human food, medicine, cultural practices and shelter, among others. Therefore, efforts to protect ecosystems and biodiversity, prevent further destruction and advance restoration, including in land and marine environments, are highly important and encouraged. This is particularly relevant in the context of biodiversity loss and given the numerous ecosystems and rich biodiversity of Singapore, due to its location in the Sundaland biodiversity hotspot. 51. Singapore is taking a leading role in the sustainability of cities. Policies and programmes are being implemented in line with the City in Nature vision. Moreover, in 2008, the Singapore Index on Cities’ Biodiversity was launched, as a self-assessment tool designed to help cities evaluate and monitor biodiversity conservation efforts over time. The tool was developed with the secretariat of the Convention on Biological Diversity and, according to information provided by the Centre for Liveable Cities during the visit, is used by almost 40 cities globally. 52. The commitment of Singapore to biodiversity conservation is embodied in its National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan. There are four legally gazetted nature reserves, covering around 3,300 hectares, corresponding to about 5 per cent of the country’s land, and another 20 areas encompassing most natural ecosystems on the island, including primary rainforest, secondary rainforest, freshwater swamp forest, streams, grasslands, sandy and rocky shores, mangrove forests, mudflats, seagrass meadows and coral reefs. 53. Most of the tropical primary forest in Singapore and a significant portion of its biodiversity was lost as a result of urban expansion and development, in particular in the nineteenth century. Therefore, preventing further biodiversity loss and prioritizing ecosystem and biodiversity restoration are fundamental. In 2020, the Government initiated the nationwide OneMillionTrees movement, to plant a million trees by 2030 to increase interconnected green spaces. Some species rehabilitation work has also borne fruit, for example, populations of threatened Oriental Pied Hornbill and Smooth-coated Otters have shown signs of recovery. During her visit, the Special Rapporteur met with several people working towards improving Singaporean biodiversity, including academics and the founder of the Woodlands Botanical Garden. Supporting and valuing their work are vital. 54. While initiatives to restore and enhance ecosystems are highly commendable, greater efforts are needed to preserve existing natural habitats and remaining primary ecosystems. It is worth pointing out that reforestation and species rehabilitation cannot fully substitute the ecological, climate and cultural value of mature and undisturbed habitats. In line with international environmental principles emphasizing in situ conservation and the precautionary principle, the protection of remaining natural areas should be prioritized. Among the measures required is the strict avoidance and refusal of projects likely to cause significant environmental harm, as the loss of intact ecosystems cannot be effectively offset through replanting or habitat creation elsewhere. 55. Mainly through land reclamation, Singapore has, over time, increased its land area by about 25 per cent. As a result, the majority of the original shore (85 per cent), mangrove forests and natural beaches have been lost, including almost two thirds of the country’s coral reefs. Lately, there have been major efforts to protect and restore marine protected areas, such as with the creation of the first marine park, the Sisters’ Islands Marine Park. During her visit to the park, the Special Rapporteur observed positive efforts to restore ecosystems, including corals and local biodiversity, and was informed of ongoing efforts to replant mangroves and seagrass and restore coastal areas. Restoring ecosystems enhances biodiversity, strengthens natural defences against flooding and sea-level rise and sustains fisheries, making them essential climate-adaptation strategies in Singapore and other low‐lying regions. These efforts for restoring marine and land ecosystems must continue and be significantly enhanced, ensuring that restoration outcomes outweigh the negative impacts of other projects, thereby generating a net positive environmental effect. 56. During the visit, the Special Rapporteur was informed by several people that the creation of some protected areas had limited access to traditional lands and traditional practices of foraging and fishing, such as for members of coastal communities, including the Orang Laut and Orang Pulau peoples. One example is the wetlands of Chek Jawa on Pulau Ubin: although its status as protected by the National Parks Board is considered a positive step by the communities, they could no longer access the beach or the water for their traditional sustainable practices. Finding ways in which the communities can use these areas for traditional, cultural and sustainable practices, including for education of younger generations, is important. 57. Co-management strategies are highly encouraged. Multiple examples worldwide show that coastal communities contribute to protecting coastal spaces, as they have a deep cultural connection to the sea. Involving coastal communities in scientific monitoring, research and considering their traditional knowledge have been shown to have positive results. Across many countries, the establishment of community-based marine management involving local coastal communities, fishers and Indigenous Peoples has supported an ecologically holistic approach to fostering ownership, securing livelihoods, preserving cultural practices and strengthening communities. A recent report by the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization on Indigenous knowledge and ancestral places also includes useful examples. 58. States must ensure that rights holders, in particular women, Indigenous Peoples, coastal and island communities, ocean defenders, small-scale fishers, children and youth, can fully and meaningfully participate in marine environmental governance at all levels. It is essential to secure preferential access and the co-management of coastal areas and resources to coastal communities, respecting free, prior and informed consent and local and traditional governance systems and guaranteeing their participation in bodies and processes relating to the ocean-climate-biodiversity nexus at all levels. 59. As a result of land reclamation, Singapore has lost several sites that supported livelihoods dependent on the sea on the outer islands, age-old fishing villages, kelongs (large, traditional offshore fishing platforms) and prawn farms. The impacts of the land reclamation strategy of Singapore extend beyond its shores, as it needs resources, such as sand, from neighbouring countries. Extensive sand dredging can cause severe environmental damage, undermining coastal protection, accelerating erosion and affecting local ecosystems and communities. This situation highlights the importance of ensuring that land reclamation projects and related sand imports are conducted in a manner that fully considers, prevents and mitigates potential transboundary environmental and social impacts – even more so when these projects are aimed at advancing climate solutions. 60. It is of great importance to prevent and minimize the impacts on ecosystems, both in Singapore and abroad, including in the face of new and upcoming projects, such as Long Island, that will imply reclaiming land. The impacts on terrestrial and marine ecosystems need to be adequately assessed and prevented, as mentioned above. Planning and its impact assessments need to be done with people’s needs taken into account and adequate access to information, public participation and access to justice. When carried out sustainably and with community support, land reclamation can help vulnerable coastal and island communities adapt to climate change. Land reclamations should consider historical damage and restoration and protect fragile marine ecosystems, in line with the obligation to protect marine ecosystems.

records.text: 48. The adaptation plan of Singapore covers resilience in the areas of food, water, public health and biodiversity. Priority adaptation measures include enhancing knowledge and expertise, coastal protection, water resource management and drainage. Dedicated finance for these measures includes the Coastal and Flood Protection Fund of 10 billion Singapore dollars (2020 to 2025) to finance coastal protection infrastructure such as sea walls and tidal gates. Complementing this, the Public Utilities Board issued green bonds in 2022, the net proceeds of which will be used to fund projects under its green financing framework. The Cooling Singapore project draws upon the collaborative efforts of researchers from various institutions to create heat resilience. Priority actions are coastal protection and improving resilience against inland and coastal flooding, taking sea level rise into account. These include ongoing site-specific studies to determine appropriate coastal protection solutions, aligning with ongoing site-specific studies and research and development, and future land reclaiming. 49. The revision by Singapore of its nationally determined contribution and its increased measures to reduce carbon emissions are efforts in the right direction. Considering its vulnerability as a small island State, it is important to align its targets to the Paris Agreement maximum limit of 1.5°C and to consider the best available science. Being a wealthy country, Singapore can contribute to identifying how further reductions in consumption-related emissions can be made, prioritizing the needs of people in vulnerable situations. In so doing, new plans and developments should consider the environmental and climate impacts on nature and people to advance sustainability and well-being, including regarding public health, for example in relation to clean air.

records.text: 42. Singapore contributes 0.1 per cent of global carbon emissions. Based on 2022 emissions, the country ranked 134th globally in terms of carbon intensity and 21st for carbon emissions per capita. Therefore, Singapore has a leading role and an opportunity to both increase its ambition in carbon-mitigation efforts and lead regionally, especially in key sectors, to motivate others to do so. In 2022, total national emissions were 58.6 metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent, from which industry-related emissions accounted for 49 per cent, power for 36.5 per cent, transport for 12 per cent, buildings for 0.9 per cent, waste and water for 0.7 per cent, households for 0.4 per cent and others for 0.5 per cent; secondary emissions had a similar distribution. 43. Singapore raised its climate ambition in its second nationally determined contribution, submitted in February 2025 to the secretariat of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, committing to reduce emissions to between 45 and 50 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent by 2035, with emissions peaking by or before 2030, and to reach net zero by 2050. The nationally determined contribution incorporates a positive change, from considering emissions intensity to absolute emissions. However, the aviation and shipping sectors are not included in the national inventories, despite being major emitting sectors. Offsetting strategies are included in the nationally determined contribution by means of carbon credits, bilateral cooperation and other measures. Although the role of international cooperation and carbon markets in achieving climate goals is recognized in the nationally determined contribution of Singapore, it remains important to continue advancing robust measures to reduce fossil fuel dependency. Continued efforts to diversify sustainable energy sources and decrease reliance on fossil fuels is essential to ensure that carbon offsets complement and do not substitute key domestic emission reductions. This approach aligns with the recommendation of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change for deep, sustained and rapid emission reductions across all systems to limit warming to 1.5°C and that carbon dioxide removal and offsetting measures cannot compensate for delayed emissions reductions in other sectors. 44. Transitioning to a lower-carbon economy has been one of the priorities of Singapore, leading to transition from coal to gas, which today corresponds to 95 per cent of its fuel generation mix (compared with about 18 per cent in 2000). The Government acknowledges that gas is a fossil fuel, albeit a less carbon-intensive one than coal. Singapore does not subsidize fossil fuel use and instead taxes it (e.g. through petrol duties) to reflect its negative externalities. Since 2020, Singapore has more than tripled its solar power deployment and is on track to achieve at least 2 gigawatt peak by 2030, which would meet about 3 per cent of the country’s total projected electricity needs. 45. Improving energy efficiency is one of the country’s main mitigation strategies, including a whole-of-government approach. The National Environment Agency actively promotes energy efficiency in the industrial, household and public sectors through legislation, incentives and public education. The Building and Construction Authority and the Land Transport Authority promote energy efficiency in the buildings and transport sectors, respectively. For example, to reduce energy consumption from air-conditioning, on which Singapore is highly dependent, on 16 May 2025, during the Special Rapporteur’s visit, the Government launched the Go25 movement, encouraging everyone to set the air‐conditioned temperature to 25°C. Natural solutions such as ventilation should also be implemented to further reduce energy consumption, while using traditional knowledge. 46. Reporting on scope 1 and 2 greenhouse gas emissions by listed companies is scheduled to start in the fiscal year 2025: over 80 per cent of companies have already disclosed these emissions in their sustainability reports. It was announced in August 2025 that reporting on scope 3 greenhouse gas emissions by Straits Times Index constituents, which collectively account for 75 per cent of total market capitalization on the Singapore Exchange, has been postponed to the fiscal year 2026. Singapore has implemented some measures to strengthen industry action and responsibility, and it is of great importance to further strengthen these comprehensive reporting systems to better monitor businesses. 47. The objective of Singapore on maritime emissions reductions relied primarily on the International Maritime Organization net-zero framework. The recent unfortunate delay in approving the framework underscores the importance of ensuring that implementing effective national measures must go hand in hand with global efforts based on international coordination to achieve meaningful reductions. Alongside its global leadership in efforts to reduce emissions, it is imperative for Singapore to strengthen its domestic efforts to mitigate emissions in the aviation and shipping sectors.

records.text: 40. The climate crisis threatens the well-being of humans and the planet, demonstrating the importance of guaranteeing a safe climate. Singapore is acutely vulnerable to climate change, which also has an impact on human rights, including to the rights to life, health, food, water, housing, an adequate standard of living and a healthy environment, cultural rights and the rights of the child. For Singapore, a small, densely populated city State, in which about one third of the land is less than 5 metres above mean sea level, climate change poses an existential threat. Sea levels are projected to rise by up to 1.15 metres by 2100 and could rise by 4 to 5 metres with the compounding effects of high tides, storm surges and land subsidence. Heat is also a big factor: 2024 was the warmest year on record, tied with 2019 and 2016. The projected increase in the average daily mean air temperature by the end of the century is between 0.6°C and 5.0°C, the number of very hot days (exceeding 33°C for an hour or more during the day) is expected to increase to between 41 and 351 annually (compared with 21 very hot days annually in the past) and more extreme rainfall (flooding) and dry spells are expected. 41. Potentially vulnerable and marginalized populations (women, children, older persons, persons with disabilities and persons living in poverty, whose adaptive capacity may be limited by marginalization) are suffering disproportionate impacts. While some information is available in Singapore documenting differentiated risks and impacts in public policy, such as the heightened vulnerability of older persons during heatwaves, it is crucial and urgent to further understand differentiated climate impacts on other groups and to integrate them into measures and policies. Special attention should be paid to documenting particular risks and impacts on children, women and persons living in poverty and other forms of vulnerability and thus facing higher risks. Such documentation is essential to develop and implement tailored and effective measures grounded in the principles of equity and non-discrimination. To do so, Singapore should consider scientific evidence analysing these differentiated impacts, including from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, United Nations entities and the special procedures.

records.text: 33. Breathing clean air is indispensable for everyone. In Singapore, air pollution sources are identified in the regulations and a network of 23 air quality monitoring stations continuously monitors six key criteria air pollutants (particulate matter (PM10), fine particulate matter (PM2.5), sulphur dioxide, ozone, carbon monoxide and nitrogen dioxide). Singapore has met its 2020 air quality targets for sulphur dioxide, nitrogen dioxide and carbon monoxide; however, as reported in official information, meeting the targets for PM10, PM2.5 and ozone levels continues to be a challenge. 34. The Pollutant Standards Index provides accurate and easily understandable information to the public about daily air-quality levels. It is available online and through a free application. In 2024, 13.5 per cent of days were in the “Good” range and 86.5 of days were in the “Moderate” range. 35. Transboundary haze, caused by forest fires in the region linked to deforestation and exacerbated by climate change, can have a negative impact on air quality in Singapore. The last significant episodes of haze occurred in 2015. They caused different impacts, including school closures to protect children’s health. As a Party to the ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution, Singapore has committed to preventing and monitoring transboundary haze pollution resulting from land and/or forest fires that should be mitigated through concerted national efforts and intensified regional and international cooperation. It is of great importance to implement the Agreement, which is instrumental in implementing effective actions against air pollution. 36. Singapore has developed early haze warnings, the measurement and dissemination of air-quality information and guidelines for dealing with haze-related issues. In 2015, it launched an investigation into companies potentially responsible for it. During the visit, the Special Rapporteur requested information about the progress and results of the investigation; she was told that it was not available as investigations were ongoing. She underlines the importance of identifying those responsible for transboundary haze and enforcing actions to prevent reoccurrence. 37. Other measures related to clean air include the effective regulation of industries by ensuring a buffer with residential areas and fitting pollution control equipment to comply with emission limits. Fuel-burning equipment must be fitted with chimneys of an approved height and emission of black smoke from chimneys is prohibited. The National Environment Agency requires regular monitoring of industry emissions. The Special Rapporteur visited Jurong Island, where many petrochemical industries are located. Continued effective regulation, enforcement measures and updated information related to industry emissions are vital, considering the potential risks for human health and the environment from such activities, for both present and future generations. 38. In Singapore, the number of vehicles and their emissions are strictly controlled under the Vehicular Emissions Regulations of the Environmental Protection and Management Act (1999), which has become progressively stricter as it has been aligned with technological advances and air-quality goals. To further reduce carbon emissions and air pollution, the Electric Vehicles Roadmap is aimed at phasing out internal combustion engine vehicles by focusing on a transition to electric vehicles and, thus, on cleaner energy by 2040. To support this, the Government offers several incentive schemes to lower the upfront costs of purchasing electric vehicles and encourage the transition. Singapore strictly controls the total vehicle population through its vehicle quota system, under which only a certain number of certificates of entitlement are permitted. This has helped curb and control the number of vehicles, which in turn helps curb air pollution. 39. Singapore is adopting strategies to address the health impacts of exposure to heat and transboundary haze, factoring in the needs of people in vulnerable situations. Such strategies include improved ventilation, the issuance of heat advisories and research on public health and the management of haze situations. Complementing existing efforts, it is vital to further consider differentiated health impacts and strengthen health-informed planning strategies, especially during worse air-quality episodes and for people in vulnerable situations. Key actions include: (a) considering the cumulative impacts of poor air quality and heat waves, as climate change increases the amount and intensity of heatwaves in Singapore; (b) prioritizing strategies, alerts and research in relation to people and groups in vulnerable situations such as children, older persons, women and outdoor workers, including construction workers; and (c) ensuring that strategies, advisories and research take into account gender, age, disability, access to health systems and other factors that could increase health risks. Implementing measures that protect public health and uphold human rights is vital to safeguarding well-being, the right to health and the right to a healthy environment.

records.section: Fulfilling the right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment
records.text: 29. Despite Singapore not expressly recognizing the right to a healthy environment in its national legislation, it has supported the United Nations and ASEAN texts recognizing this right. Hence, advancing the implementation of the right is fundamental. 30. Given that the International Court of Justice concluded that it was difficult to see how the obligations to guarantee the effective enjoyment of human rights could be fulfilled without at the same time ensuring the protection of the right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment, it is fundamental for Singapore to ensure the protection of the right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment as a human right. 31. The right to a healthy environment is compound and includes substantive and procedural elements. The substantive elements encompass clean air, safe and sufficient water, healthy and sustainably produced food, a non-toxic environment, healthy biodiversity and ecosystems and a safe climate. The procedural elements, also recognized as human rights, are access to environmental information, public participation in environmental decision‐making processes and access to justice with adequate remedies. These elements are interconnected; therefore, programmes, policies and projects must be implemented taking an intersectional, integrated and comprehensive approach. 32. The Committee on the Rights of the Child, in its general comment No. 26 (2023), clarified the obligations of States to address environmental harm and climate change, emphasizing the urgent need to address the adverse effects of environmental degradation, especially in the context of climate change and the enjoyment of children’s rights. The Committee also explained how rights under the Convention on the Rights of the Child applied to environmental protection and confirmed that children had a right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment.

records.section: Environmental, social and human rights impact assessments
records.text: 25. Singapore takes a systematic and science-based approach to assessing and mitigating the environmental impacts of development projects through its domestic Environmental Impact Assessment Framework, which is part of the planning and evaluation processes administered through the Urban Redevelopment Authority. Technical agencies assess the expected environmental impacts of development projects. 26. According to information provided during the visit, projects with significant impact are subject to further studies and “mitigation measures are put in place where necessary”. Reports from environmental impact assessments are “publicly available online, unless there are specific reasons to maintain confidentiality like security considerations”. The existing Singaporean Environmental Impact Assessment Framework, including its processes, timelines and consultations with community stakeholders, is determined by technical agencies and applicable guidelines on a case-by-case basis and development proposals are expected to meet existing regulatory requirements under various environmental protection‐related legislation. Currently, there is no specific law regulating these assessments. 27. The Special Rapporteur strongly encourages Singapore to further regulate environmental impact assessment processes and guarantee that all projects, including those related to development and climate adaptation, are thoroughly and comprehensively evaluated prior to starting. Her report to the General Assembly at its eightieth session provides a framework for environmental, social and human rights impact assessments for States to comply with their obligations to regulate, undertake, monitor and enforce these assessments, while ensuring adequate access to information, public participation and access to justice and effective remedies. As explained in that report, environmental, social and human rights impact assessment processes must: (a) Be undertaken as early as possible and prior to the commencement of a project; (b) Comprehensively assess direct, indirect, domestic, transboundary, adverse, positive, cumulative, short- and long-term, climate, biodiversity, environmental, health, cultural, social and human rights impacts; (c) Follow precautionary, prevention, proportionality, best available science, maximum disclosure and equity and non-discrimination principles; (d) Be independent; (e) Ensure access to information, public participation and access to justice and special measures for the protection of the rights of marginalized people. 28. It is vital that environmental, social and human rights impact assessments are clearly regulated and specify, at a minimum: (a) The full range of activities and associated impacts, specifying physical and technical characteristics (including geographical and ecosystem sensitivity) and analysing a no-action baseline among any other project alternatives; (b) The applicable procedure, including how access to information, public participation and access to justice will be guaranteed; (c) The delineation of responsibilities and duties across proponents, authorities, experts conducting assessments and decision makers; (d) How assessments will inform and govern decisions regarding proposed activities and monitoring; (e) The steps and measures to be adopted in the event of non-compliance; (f) Assessments for modifications of approved projects, including expansions.

records.section: Long-term planning for present and future generations
records.text: 21. Planning is central in Singapore, as evidenced by its long-term 50-year plans, followed up by master plans covering a 10- to 15-year period, regularly reviewed every 5 years. Current planning is defined in the Long-Term Plan Review 2021 and the Draft Master Plan 2025, both of which include references to restoring the environment and nature and to climate change and urbanization as the links between a good-quality living environment and city resilience. At the same time, these plans include major growth projects, such as the expansion of Changi airport with an additional terminal to accommodate 50 million more travellers, making a total of 140 million passengers per year, the Long Island reclamation project and the industrial development projects in the West Region, including Tuas Port, Jurong Lake District and Jurong Innovation District. 22. Considering the ambitious plans for the next 50 years, and the potential significant environmental, social and human rights impacts that these might have, as they include infrastructure projects such as increasing housing, port–industry integration and synergistic industries, increasing the green economy and innovation and becoming a world-leading hub for aerospace and digital and cybersecurity industries, it is fundamental that the Long-Term Plan, the Master Plan and all planning efforts are updated based on the best available science, considering planetary boundaries and impacts on the environment, climate and human rights, including public health and present and future generations. These efforts and activities must also include comprehensive impact assessments. 23. In 2021, the Singapore Green Plan 2030 was launched “to galvanize a whole-of-nation movement and advance Singapore’s national agenda on sustainable development”. The Plan is aimed at strengthening the efforts of Singapore to implement the Paris Agreement and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. It includes sectoral plans and targets over the next 10 years to achieve long-term net-zero emission targets and build up its climate, resource and economic resilience. The Green Plan contains targets that will enhance food security, ensure sustainable water management, scale up the deployment of clean energy, promote sustainable economic growth and green infrastructure and industries and position the city to be resource-efficient and climate-resilient. The Green Plan also includes targets for the public sector. 24. Although the Long-Term Plan is aimed at protecting present and future generations, it does not fully include all environmental and climate goals considered in the Green Plan, the 2030 Agenda and international climate and environmental commitments. Although the long-term development plans of Singapore are periodically reviewed, further alignment between the long- and midterm plans and the Green Plan is crucial to promote coherence and advance consistent, integrated actions to better consider and protect present and future generations’ rights.

records.text: 18. Singapore has developed a highly technical system of environmental regulations, aiming to balance rapid development with sustainability. Agencies such as the National Environment Agency and the Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment enforce laws covering pollution control, waste management and water protection. Key legislation, such as the Prevention of Pollution of the Sea Act (1990), the Hazardous Waste Act (1997), the Environmental Protection and Management Act (1999), the Energy Conservation Act (2012), the Carbon Pricing Act (2018) and the Resource Sustainability Act (2019), requires industries and individuals to adopt practices aiming to prevent environmental degradation. Existing penalties for non-compliance reinforce accountability and, in general, the domestic legal framework reflects the objective of sustainable growth and environmental protection for future generations and contains some basic references to how environmental degradation and climate change have an impact on human health. Fully integrating human rights- and ecosystem-based approaches into policies and regulations will contribute to complementing the existing technical-scientific perspective, so that green and blue spaces support natural ecosystems and increase well-being, as described below. 19. The National Environment Agency is responsible for the formulation and enforcement of environmental policies and regulations. It oversees a broad spectrum of environmental issues, including air and water quality management, waste management, industrial pollution regulation, energy efficiency, measures to mitigate hydrofluorocarbons and other climate change measures. It conducts regular inspections and audits to ensure that businesses comply with established environmental standards and practices. It also manages pollution control measures and is responsible for the effective implementation of environmental laws, thereby mitigating adverse impacts on public health, the environment and the climate. 20. The Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment serves as the overarching authority responsible for all matters related to environmental sustainability. It oversees the National Environment Agency and focuses on policy development concerning environmental conservation, climate change mitigation and resource management. It plays a critical role in facilitating inter-agency coordination and public engagement.

records.text: 16. The Constitution of Singapore was first adopted in 1959 and has since undergone multiple amendments, the most recent in 2010. Following independence from Malaysia on 9 August 1965, a provisional constitution was enacted on 22 December 1965, comprising three documents: (a) the Constitution of the State of Singapore 1963; (b) the Republic of Singapore Independence Act 1965; and (c) parts of the Malaysian Federal Constitution incorporated through the Independence Act. In March 1980, the Attorney General issued a consolidated reprint of the Constitution, integrating all amendments into a single unified document. 17. In the Constitution, the focus on fundamental liberties is on civil and political rights; the environment is not mentioned. The Government’s position, as observed by legal scholars, is that effective environmental management can be achieved through laws and regulations without the need for a constitutional environmental right. While constitutional recognition has been done in the majority of States globally to mainstream the right and add clarity, legal recognition is another option that can help with understanding of the elements of the right and how to better interpret them in the national context.

records.text: 14. The right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment is a fundamental human right, as recognized by the General Assembly in its resolution 76/300 and the Human Rights Council in its resolution 48/13. Singapore voted in favour of the General Assembly resolution, joining 160 other States on that historical vote. In addition, as mentioned above, Singapore agreed to the adoption of the 2025 ASEAN Declaration on the Right to a Safe, Clean, Healthy and Sustainable Environment, which contains an express recognition of that right. Currently, the human right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment is not expressly included in the domestic legal framework of Singapore; however, national regulations incorporate some of the elements of that right. 15. Advancing the recognition and implementation of the human right to a safe, clean, healthy and sustainable environment is fundamental, considering that, as the International Court of Justice concluded, it is a precondition of, inherent in and essential for the effective enjoyment of all human rights, given the interdependence between human rights and the protection of the environment. Therefore, the Special Rapporteur emphasizes the importance of Singapore considering reviewing its national legal framework and expressly recognizing the human right to a healthy environment, incorporating it into policies and regulations. Singapore should also cooperate with other ASEAN States to apply the Declaration through the regional plan of action.

records.text: 8. Singapore has ratified four of the nine main human rights conventions: the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination, the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women, the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities and the Convention on the Rights of the Child, as well as the Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Rights of the Child on the involvement of children in armed conflict. 9. Singapore is a founding member of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), which, in 2012, adopted the ASEAN Human Rights Declaration, which contains a reference to the right to a safe, clean and sustainable environment. A recent positive development is the adoption of the ASEAN Declaration on the Right to a Safe, Clean, Healthy and Sustainable Environment, on 26 October 2025. The explicit recognition of the human right to a safe, clean, healthy and sustainable environment is a fundamental step forward in addressing the triple planetary crisis. The Special Rapporteur has been collaborating with the process and looks forward to the regional plan of action, a process that must be participatory and inclusive and to which she remains available to contribute. The effective implementation of the Declaration should be aligned with and reinforce existing norms in multilateral environmental agreements. It should strengthen the role of business and the protection of human rights defenders and improve public participation, access to information and access to justice and remedy. 10. Singapore is a Party to the following international environmental agreements: the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, the Kyoto Protocol, the Paris Agreement, the Basel Convention on the Control of Transboundary Movements of Hazardous Wastes and Their Disposal, the Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants, the Rotterdam Convention on the Prior Informed Consent Procedure for Certain Hazardous Chemicals and Pesticides in International Trade, the Minamata Convention on Mercury and the Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer. 11. Singapore was crucial in the drafting of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, adopted in 1982, and fundamental in achieving the Agreement under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea on the Conservation and Sustainable Use of Marine Biological Diversity of Areas beyond National Jurisdiction, which will enter into force in January 2026. It was ratified by Singapore in September 2024. 12. Singapore, as all other States, has the erga omnes obligation to prevent significant environmental harm, according to the International Court of Justice. The obligation to effectively regulate, control, monitor and enforce activities that might cause significant environmental harm derives from that. In its submission to the Court on 20 March 2024, Singapore argued that the obligation to prevent environmental harm was customary international law, adding that the obligation extended to significant environmental harm caused to areas beyond national control. The Court agreed with that perspective, as argued by the majority of States. It is important for Singapore to ensure the inclusion thereof in its national legal framework, including planning and regulations, as well as in its contributions in regional and international multilateral forums. 13. Singapore has taken an active part in multilateral cooperation, including that aimed at advancing environmental protection internationally. For example, the Singapore Cooperation Programme provides capacity-building in areas such as water, sanitation and sustainable urban development. In 2022, Singapore introduced the Sustainability Action Package to further support developing countries in addressing sustainability and climate challenges. The Package is focused on decarbonization, strengthening water and food security, financing and managing green projects, developing sustainable infrastructure and advancing carbon market management.

Recalling its general recommendation No. 21 (1994) on equality in marriage and family relations and its general recommendation No. 29 (2013) on the economic consequences of marriage, family relations and their dissolution, the Committee recommends that the State party: (a) Ensure that women have an equal right with men to enter into marriage, without having to resort to court proceedings to secure that right, by abolishing the requirement for women to obtain permission from a male guardian; (b) Explicitly prohibit polygamy and ensure the protection of the economic rights of women in existing polygamous unions; (c) Ensure that women have equal rights with men to divorce and to inheritance; (d) Set the minimum age of marriage at 18 years for both women and men, without exceptions, and address the root causes of child marriage, including patriarchal attitudes and gender stereotypes; encourage reporting of child marriage and ensure the prosecution and adequate punishment of those responsible for child marriage, including complicit family members, religious and community leaders, and civil registrars, in accordance with joint general recommendation No. 31 of the Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women/general comment No. 18 of the Committee on the Rights of the Child (2019) on harmful practices, as revised; (e) Recognize the equal right of all women, including those in same-sex relationships and non-married women, to parenthood through assisted reproductive technology, and ensure that all children enjoy equal rights to citizenship regardless of their family circumstances.

records.section: Climate change and disaster risk reduction
records.text: 58. The Committee recommends that, in line with its general recommendation No. 37 (2018) on the gender-related dimensions of disaster risk reduction in the context of climate change, the State party review its climate change and disaster response strategies, taking into account the negative effects of climate change on the livelihoods of women, and ensure that women are equally represented with men in the development, adoption and implementation of legislation, policies and programmes on climate change, disaster response and disaster risk reduction, in particular by: (a) Ensuring the incorporation of a gender perspective in climate change and disaster risk reduction legislation, policies, financing and programmes, including economic infrastructure sectors and the green economy, renewable energy and clean technology; and empowering women by equipping them with knowledge to effectively participate in climate change-related decision-making and the development of adaptation strategies and actions that build women’s and girls’ resilience to the impacts of climate change; (b) Introducing effective gender budgeting for climate financing and climate change adaptation activities, including those aimed at financing and encouraging a sustainable blue economy, to ensure that such initiatives are fully inclusive of women, promote women’s empowerment and support the climate change agenda to help women and girls adapt effectively to climate change and disasters; (c) Promoting women’s active participation in the creation and implementation of new funding arrangements for responding to environmental damage, as decided during the twenty-seventh session of the Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, held in 2022.

The Committee notes the position of the State party concerning its reservation to article 11 (2) of the Convention “that legislation in respect of article 11 is unnecessary for the minority of women who do not fall within the ambit of Singapore’s employment legislation”. However, the Committee notes that foreign work permit holders constitute 30 per cent of the State party’s workforce, including a large proportion of women migrant domestic workers. It notes with concern: (a) That migrant domestic workers, most of whom are migrant women, are not covered under the Employment Act, but rather under the Employment of Foreign Manpower Act, which lacks protections of basic labour rights, including limitations on working hours and provisions for overtime pay, annual leave and medical leave, and exposes them to economic and physical abuse, risk of trafficking and exploitation; (b) The absence of specific legislation regulating domestic employment that includes provisions regarding the effective protection of migrant domestic workers from abuse, exploitation and violence, or that provides for labour inspections of domestic households, and the absence of penalties imposed on employers for withholding the passports of migrant domestic workers, despite legislation prohibiting that practice, or for failing to provide adequate housing, food, medical expenses, daily breaks and weekly rest days; (c) The absence of effective complaint mechanisms with adequate enforcement measures against employers engaging in abusive practices and the denial of the right of women migrant domestic workers to obtain redress for wrongful dismissals from the Employment Claims Tribunal; (d) That it is currently illegal for women migrant workers, including migrant domestic workers, to become pregnant and that they are subject to mandatory and regular testing for pregnancy and are deported when pregnancy is detected.

Recalling its general recommendation No. 36 (2017) on the right of girls and women to education, the Committee recommends that the State party raise awareness of the importance of girls’ education as a basis for their empowerment, and: (a) Raise awareness among parents, teachers, traditional and religious leaders, women, men, girls and boys of the importance of girls’ and women’s education to their economic empowerment, personal development and autonomy; combat structural barriers that deter girls from choosing non ‐ traditional fields of study, such as science, technology, engineering and mathematics, and information and communications technology; and address the high dropout rate of women on career paths related to science, technology, engineering and mathematics (“leaky pipeline phenomenon”) ; (b) Develop national policies to ensure that progress in education for women and girls translates into improved employment prospects for them; promote and encourage girls and women to enrol in non-traditional fields of study, such as science, technology, engineering and mathematics, and information and communications technology, including through orientation programmes and career counselling in secondary and higher education; and support the development of leadership skills, critical thinking and the ability to lead and take decisions among women and girls, including for emerging green jobs, green engineering solutions and green finance; (c) Strengthen regulations on the protection of pupils, including girls, from harassment, disinformation, cyberviolence and cyberbullying; raise awareness of the risks of cyberviolence and cyberbullying a mong students, parents, teachers and the general public; and monitor the adoption of zero-tolerance policies for handling cases of harassment and cyberbullying of students, including girls; (d) Strengthen the effective implementation of comprehensive sexuality education at all levels of education and ensure that it includes: (i) inclusive and accessible content on gender equality, including on women’s rights and the harmful effects of gender-based violence against women and girls; (ii) age-appropriate sexuality education, with particular attention paid to the concept of consent, responsible sexual behaviour and the prevention of early pregnancies and sexually transmitted diseases; and (iii) education on human rights and peace; (e) Take measures, including temporary special measures, such as financial incentives, special scholarships and tax exemptions for employers, to ensure that women migrant workers, including women migrant domestic workers, and all women and girls belonging to vulnerable and marginalized communities have access to education and vocational training.

records.text: 41. The Committee notes with appreciation the State party’s significant efforts in the field of education. records.section: Trafficking in women and exploitation of prostitution
records.text: 36. Recalling its general recommendation No. 38 (2020) on trafficking in women and girls in the context of global migration, the Committee recommends that the State party: (a) Ensure that all cases of trafficking, including sex trafficking, are investigated and prosecuted and that perpetrators and their accomplices receive sentences that are commensurate with the gravity of the crime; (b) Amend the Prevention of Human Trafficking Act to incorporate the principle of non-punishment of victims of trafficking and ensure that all women and girls who are victims of trafficking, without exception, are exempt from arrest, detention, prosecution and punishment for irregular entry or stay in the State party, lack of documentation or for their involvement in unlawful activities to the extent that such involvement is a direct consequence of their situation as victims of trafficking; (c) Ensure that victims of trafficking can report their cases without fear of deportation or retribution; (d) Provide capacity-building for the judiciary, law enforcement officials, immigration officers, border guards and social workers to ensure that victims of trafficking, including women migrant domestic workers, are not inadvertently placed in detention or subject to removal procedures, and that the national legal and policy framework to combat trafficking in women and girls and gender-sensitive procedures for the early identification and referral of victims to appropriate services are implemented; (e) Strengthen capacity-building for law enforcement officials and cooperation with civil society organizations, including through strengthening their human, technical and financial resources, to ensure that victims of trafficking are identified, assisted and protected at an early stage, including through the operation of mobile units, and to guarantee the implementation of safe disclosure procedures and the availability safe spaces , targeting in particular sites where displaced and migrant women and girls are accommodated, registered or detained; (f) Ensure the systematic collection and analysis of data on trafficking, disaggregated by age, sex, nationality of victims and forms of trafficking.

records.text: 35. The Committee notes the State party’s efforts to strengthen its legal and policy framework to combat trafficking in women and girls and implement its National Approach Against Trafficking in Persons (2016–2026). However, it remains concerned that the State party continues to be a destination and transit country for trafficking in persons, in particular women and girls, for purposes of sexual and labour exploitation. In particular, the Committee notes with concern: (a) That, despite the fact that the Prevention of Human Trafficking Act meets the definition of the Protocol to Prevent, Suppress and Punish Trafficking in Persons, Especially Women and Children, supplementing the United Nations Convention against Transnational Organized Crime, there have been no prosecutions and convictions under the Act since 2020; (b) The lack of a provision in the Prevention of Human Trafficking Act on the right of victims of trafficking not to be prosecuted for legal infractions (so-called non‐punishment clause); (c) The lack of coordinated efforts, including legislative and policy measures, to eliminate trafficking for the purpose of labour exploitation of women migrant domestic workers, and the insufficient priority given to the prevention and identification of risk factors in the State party; (d) The limited awareness among police and other law enforcement officers about trafficking indicators, including signs of coercion, such as passport retention, debt bondage, non-payment of wages and forced confinement, as well as the lack of gender-sensitive procedures for dealing with victims of trafficking; (e) The lack of cooperation with civil society organizations on victim identification and assistance.

Recalling its general recommendation No. 35 (2017) on gender-based violence against women, updating general recommendation No. 19, the Committee recommends that the State party: (a) Adopt legislation to ensure that all forms of gender-based violence against women, including domestic violence and online violence, are specifically criminalized, and take into account the special protection needs of disadvantaged and marginalized groups of women, including women with disabilities, migrant women, older women, and lesbian, bisexual, transgender and intersex women; (b) Strengthen the implementation of the Online Criminal Harms Act, the Online Safety (Miscellaneous Amendments) Act and other regulatory procedures and due diligence mechanisms to hold social media companies accountable for user-generated content used in incidents of online violence and harassment and for the prompt removal of such content; ensure that such companies have effective reporting mechanisms; and ensure that there are processes in place for the State party to bring perpetrators of online violence and harassment to justice; (c) Intensify awareness-raising for the general public on the criminal nature of all forms of gender-based violence, including domestic and sexual violence, and on the need to enable women to report such cases without fear of reprisals, stigmatization or revictimization; (d) Ensure that women and girls who are survivors of gender-based violence have access to affordable and, if necessary, free legal aid; ease the burden of proof on complainants; ensure affordable access to forensic evidence; and continue to build the capacity of judges, prosecutors, the police and other law enforcement officers on gender-sensitive investigation and interrogation methods in cases of gender-based violence against women; (e) Strengthen victim support services and protection, including through the provision of a 24/7 hotline, adequate and accessible shelters, medical treatment, psychosocial counselling and economic support to women and girls victims of gender-based violence in the State party.

The Committee stresses that female genital mutilation, female circumcision and female genital cutting cannot be justified on religious grounds and constitute a harmful practice that seeks to assert male control over women’s and girls’ bodies and sexuality and violates the Convention, irrespective of whether or not these practices are performed within or outside a medical institution. It recommends that the State party: (a) Criminalize all forms of female genital mutilation, ensuring that such criminalization cannot be overruled by fatwas or other rulings issued by religious or clerical authorities, in accordance with joint general recommendation No. 31 of the Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women/general comment No. 18 of the Committee on the Rights of the Child (2019), as revised, on harmful practices, and target 5.3 of the Sustainable Development Goals; (b) Conduct awareness-raising and educational campaigns, in particular among medical staff, practitioners, parents, community leaders, religious scholars, women and girls, and men and boys, aimed at promoting understanding of the criminal nature of and the need to eliminate female genital mutilation; (c) Provide victims and at-risk women and girls with information about available mechanisms to file complaints against perpetrators of female genital mutilation and ensure their access to legal aid and quality social and rehabilitation services; (d) Strengthen data collection on the number of women and girls who have been subjected to female genital mutilation or cutting for purposes of the design and implementation of tailored and gender-responsive legislation, policies, programmes and budgets.

records.text: 56. The Committee recommends that the State party: (a) Promote the participation of persons with disabilities, including women with disabilities, in political and public decision-making processes at all levels and in political life in general; (b) Ensure that electoral and voting procedures, facilities, and print and online election material are accessible in all formats, such as Braille, plain language, Easy Read and sign language, or are available on accessible websites; (c) Guarantee that all organizations of persons with disabilities and their members are able to participate in political and public life on an equal basis with others, irrespective of their views on the Government’s policies regarding the implementation of the Convention, and that they do not face any intimidation, retribution or repression whatsoever from the Government or other public entities; (d) Ensure that representatives of all organizations of persons with disabilities, irrespective of their views on the Government’s policies regarding the implementation of the Convention, are able to participate in the State party reporting procedure without fear of intimidation, retribution or repression.

records.text: 52. The Committee recalls its general comment No. 8 (2022) and target 8.5 of the Sustainable Development Goals, and recommends that the State party: (a) Adopt legislation and time-bound policies and benchmarks to ensure that persons with disabilities have access to work and employment in the open labour market and are included in private and public work environments, on an equal basis with others, and move towards eradicating sheltered workshops; (b) Undertake a comprehensive review of the Tripartite Alliance for Fair and Progressive Employment Practices, including establishing a comprehensive definition of disability, prohibiting direct and indirect discrimination and recognizing the denial of reasonable accommodation as a form of prohibited discrimination, and establish an effective mechanism for implementation and monitoring to provide redress in case of non-compliance; (c) Expand the Open Door Programme to provide longer-term support, in particular for persons with disabilities taking part in deinstitutionalization processes, autistic persons, persons with intellectual disabilities and persons with psychosocial disabilities; (d) Extend the jurisdiction of the employment claims tribunals to all claims about violations of the right to work and employment of persons with disabilities, and establish an accessible and confidential mechanism to report such violations; (e) Combat attitudinal barriers among private and public employers and apply universal design in all work-related environments.
